architectural_implications.observation: Safety-critical decisions are moved out of the prompt and into a deterministic pre-model layer.

architectural_implications.after: Scheduled automated judges run every few hours over live traffic on clinical accuracy, safety, and escalation correctness, alongside per-message feedback and 100% sampling of high-stakes cases.
architectural_implications.before: A launch gate reviews quality once; subsequent model or prompt changes ship with limited regression coverage.
architectural_implications.consequence: New failure modes introduced by version changes are caught in production trends, but the team must staff human reviewers to read and act on the resulting signals.
architectural_implications.observation: Evaluation is promoted from a pre-launch checklist to a continuously running production subsystem.

architectural_implications.before: PHI handling and environment separation are treated as policy or downstream filtering concerns.

architectural_implications.observation: Compliance boundaries are enforced at data-flow seams rather than at the model.

article_ideas.based_on: A model is not a guardrail, and a system prompt is not code
article_ideas.thesis: Any safety control expressed as a system prompt is probabilistic by construction and therefore not a control at all; must-not-fail behaviors such as crisis escalation, identity verification, and intent routing must be deterministic branches that execute before model invocation and can short-circuit it entirely.

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Stripping PHI at the pipeline boundary before data reaches the data lake
deep_dives.why: Boundary enforcement bounds regulatory exposure structurally, but the price is paid later and less visibly: fewer debuggable traces, less representative training data, and slower reproduction of production failures. summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Rashi Agrawal
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Guardrails and decisioning frameworks for building member-facing health AI systems
  • Purpose: To provide practitioners with concrete architectural patterns and decision-making frameworks for deploying member-facing healthcare AI safely and compliantly. Rashi Agrawal, Head of AI and ML at Hinge Health, discusses the critical guardrails and architectural principles needed to build safe, member-facing healthcare AI. Drawing on real-world industry incidents like AI chatbots giving dangerous medical advice, Agrawal presents a three-layer architectural approach and a five-rule decisioning framework to ensure safety, reliability, and human trust in healthcare AI deployments.

Topic Map

The State of Healthcare AI and Safety Risks

  • Explanation: Overview of real-world AI failures in healthcare, such as incorrect dietary advice and under-triaging life-threatening emergencies.
  • Key claims:
    • 40 million people use frontier models for health issues
    • Recent high-profile incidents highlight dangerous chatbot medical errors
    • ECRI ranked AI chatbot misuse as the number one health technology hazard of 2026
  • Examples:
    • A 60-year-old man instructed to replace salt with sodium bromide by an AI chatbot, leading to hospitalization
    • Consumer health AI under-triaging life-threatening emergencies like diabetic ketoacidosis 50% of the time
  • Terminology:
    • PHI (Protected Health Information)
    • LLM
    • triage
    • frontier models
  • Why it matters: Shows that healthcare AI cannot rely solely on probabilistic model outputs because the stakes involve human life and severe regulatory penalties.

The Three Non-Negotiable Foundations

  • Explanation: Core architectural principles required before shipping healthcare AI: constraint as architecture, deterministic rules above probabilistic models, and safety as a continuous evaluation layer.
  • Key claims:
    • Most AI safety failures are architectural decisions made before a single token was generated
    • Deterministic rules must live above the model, not inside it
    • Safety is a continuous evaluation layer, not a one-time gate
  • Examples:
    • Stripping PHI at the pipeline boundary before data reaches the data lake
    • Hard isolation between production and non-production environments
  • Terminology:
    • probabilistic systems
    • deterministic rules
    • evaluation layer
    • production baseline
  • Why it matters: Establishes that safety must be built into the system architecture from day one rather than patched on via prompts.

Code Layer vs. Model Layer (Layer 1 and Layer 2)

  • Explanation: Detailed breakdown of enforcing policy via architecture and placing must-not-fail behaviors in the code layer above prompts.
  • Key claims:
    • A model is not a guardrail, and a system prompt is not code
    • Probabilistic systems excel at generation but fail at must-not-fail rules
    • Every turn goes through the code layer first before reaching the model
  • Examples:
    • Emergency escalation routing for self-harm or suicidal ideation directly to 911 or 988 in code
    • Intent routing and identity verification handled by deterministic code
  • Terminology:
    • code layer
    • model layer
    • prompt injection
    • irreversible decisions
  • Why it matters: Ensures critical high-stakes routing and authentication are never left to probability or vulnerable to prompt overrides.

Safety as a Continuous Evaluation Layer (Layer 3)

  • Explanation: Why pre-launch checklists are insufficient and how production automated judges, member feedback, and sampled traces maintain safety over time.
  • Key claims:
    • Safety is a continuous evaluation layer that runs the whole time
    • Automated judges must run on live production traffic with multiple dimensions
    • The bottleneck is having enough people to read signals and act on them
  • Examples:
    • Automated judges checking clinical accuracy, safety, and escalation correctness every few hours
    • Thumbs up/down member feedback on every message
    • 100% sampling on high-stake cases
  • Terminology:
    • automated judges
    • member feedback
    • sampled traces
    • regression
  • Why it matters: Proves that monitoring is the first resort for catching new failures and scaling safety with new judges as consumer usage grows.

The Decisioning Framework (5 Rules for Stakeholder Disagreements)

  • Explanation: A structured framework for resolving launch disagreements across clinical, legal, compliance, product, and engineering stakeholders.
  • Key claims:
    • Worst case wins: Severity is set by the worst plausible outcome, not the average
    • Severity does not equal capacity: A bug's severity is determined by harm, not team capacity
    • Asymmetric default: When in doubt, default to the safer mistake
    • Revealed tolerance beats stated tolerance: Align with actual accepted production behavior
    • Humans are the constraint: Always design for the human in the loop
  • Examples:
    • Comparing safety bugs (always hold and fix) versus polished bugs (ship)
    • Evaluating clinical risk vs velocity risk prior to launch
  • Terminology:
    • worst case
    • asymmetric default
    • revealed tolerance
    • human in the loop
  • Why it matters: Resolves organizational deadlock when five different stakeholders see five different risks during product launches.

Key Points

Constraint is the Architecture

  • Explanation: Safety failures stem from architectural design choices made before model deployment, not just model failures.
  • Evidence: ECRI ranking AI chatbot misuse as the top health tech hazard for 2026.
  • Practical implication: Architect systems so that PHI is stripped at ingestion and environments are strictly isolated.

Must-Not-Fail Belongs Above the Prompt

  • Explanation: Probabilistic models are unreliable for deterministic business logic and critical safety checks.
  • Evidence: Code layer runs first on every turn; models never get a vote on high-stakes calls.
  • Practical implication: Implement emergency routing and authentication checks in deterministic code rather than system prompts.

Safety is Continuous, Not a Gate

  • Explanation: Pre-launch evaluation checklists are necessary but insufficient for production AI systems.
  • Evidence: New model versions and prompt changes introduce new failures over time.
  • Practical implication: Deploy continuous automated judges, live member feedback monitoring, and 100% sampled traces.

Worst Case Wins in Healthcare Decisions

  • Explanation: When evaluating bug severity, the worst plausible outcome sets the standard, not the average case.
  • Evidence: A bug causing serious harm to 0.1% of users is much worse than a minor annoyance to 100%.
  • Practical implication: Never compromise on safety bugs for velocity; treat fast-follows as committed debt.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

Three-Layer Architecture for Member-Facing Health AI

  • How it works: Combines policy-enforcing architecture, deterministic code layers for high-stakes logic, and continuous safety evaluation layers in production.
  • Components:
    • Layer 1: Pipeline sanitization and environment isolation
    • Layer 2: Code layer running above prompts for deterministic safety rules
    • Layer 3: Continuous evaluation layer with automated judges, member feedback, and sampled traces
  • When to use: When building member-facing healthcare AI or any high-stakes regulated AI application.

The Five-Rule Decisioning Framework

  • How it works: A decision-making model to resolve launch blockages when cross-functional stakeholders disagree on risk.
  • Components:
    • Rule 1: Worst case wins
    • Rule 2: Severity does not equal capacity
    • Rule 3: Asymmetric default (safety first)
    • Rule 4: Revealed tolerance over stated tolerance
    • Rule 5: Humans are the constraint
  • When to use: When deciding whether to ship, delay, or fix features when clinical, legal, compliance, product, and engineering stakeholders disagree.

Examples & Case Studies

A 60-year-old healthy man asked a popular AI assistant how to cut salt and was told to use sodium bromide, leading to hospitalization.

  • Illustrates: The danger of probabilistic models generating hallucinatory medical advice without deterministic safety boundaries.
  • Lesson: High-stakes medical guidance cannot be left to probabilistic generation.

An independent safety test out of Mount Sinai found health AI under-triaged life-threatening emergencies 50% of the time.

  • Illustrates: Current consumer health AI safety gaps and production baseline risks.
  • Lesson: Rigorous architectural guardrails and deterministic triage pathways are required.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Sanitize PHI at the pipeline boundary before storage
    • Place deterministic safety rules in code above prompts
    • Evaluate models continuously using live production traffic and automated judges
  • Strategic:
    • Adopt the worst-case mindset for healthcare AI safety evaluation
    • Align launch decisions with revealed organizational tolerance rather than stated goals
    • Treat fast-follows as committed debt rather than optional backlog items
  • Questions to investigate:
    • Are our high-stakes safety checks handled in code or left to system prompts?
    • Do we have continuous automated judges evaluating live production traffic?
    • How do we resolve launch disagreements between clinical, legal, and engineering stakeholders?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • 40 million people use frontier models for triaging healthcare issues (statistic)
  • ECRI named AI chatbot misuse the number one health technology hazard of 2026 (industry report)

Notable Quotes

"So how do you ship AI to someone who has already trusted you with their health?" (at 0:53) "A model is not a guardrail. A model with a system prompt is not a guardrail. Code that runs above the model is closer." (at 10:15) "Architecture is how. Decisioning is when. Member trust is why." (at 35:02)

Compressed Summary

  • healthcare ai requires strict architectural guardrails and deterministic code layers
  • must-not-fail logic like emergency routing must live above prompts in code
  • safety is a continuous production evaluation layer using automated judges and member feedback
  • the 5-rule decisioning framework resolves stakeholder launch conflicts using worst-case analysis
  • Keywords: guardrails, healthcare, architecture, safety, decisioning
  • Core insight: Building trusted healthcare AI requires enforcing non-negotiable safety rules through architecture and deterministic code rather than relying solely on model prompts and probabilistic generation.

- **Key claims**:
  - 40 million people use frontier models for health issues
  - Recent high-profile incidents highlight dangerous chatbot medical errors
  - ECRI ranked AI chatbot misuse as the number one health technology hazard of 2026
- **Examples**:
  - A 60-year-old man instructed to replace salt with sodium bromide by an AI chatbot, leading to hospitalization
  - Consumer health AI under-triaging life-threatening emergencies like diabetic ketoacidosis 50% of the time
- **Terminology**:
  - PHI (Protected Health Information)
  - LLM
  - triage
  - frontier models
- **Why it matters**: Shows that healthcare AI cannot rely solely on probabilistic model outputs because the stakes involve human life and severe regulatory penalties.
### The Three Non-Negotiable Foundations
- **Explanation**: Core architectural principles required before shipping healthcare AI: constraint as architecture, deterministic rules above probabilistic models, and safety as a continuous evaluation layer.
- **Key claims**:
  - Most AI safety failures are architectural decisions made before a single token was generated
  - Deterministic rules must live above the model, not inside it
  - Safety is a continuous evaluation layer, not a one-time gate
- **Examples**:
  - Stripping PHI at the pipeline boundary before data reaches the data lake
  - Hard isolation between production and non-production environments
- **Terminology**:
  - probabilistic systems
  - deterministic rules
  - evaluation layer
  - production baseline
- **Why it matters**: Establishes that safety must be built into the system architecture from day one rather than patched on via prompts.
### Code Layer vs. Model Layer (Layer 1 and Layer 2)
- **Explanation**: Detailed breakdown of enforcing policy via architecture and placing must-not-fail behaviors in the code layer above prompts.
- **Key claims**:
  - A model is not a guardrail, and a system prompt is not code
  - Probabilistic systems excel at generation but fail at must-not-fail rules
  - Every turn goes through the code layer first before reaching the model
- **Examples**:
  - Emergency escalation routing for self-harm or suicidal ideation directly to 911 or 988 in code
  - Intent routing and identity verification handled by deterministic code
- **Terminology**:
  - code layer
  - model layer
  - prompt injection
  - irreversible decisions
- **Why it matters**: Ensures critical high-stakes routing and authentication are never left to probability or vulnerable to prompt overrides.
### Safety as a Continuous Evaluation Layer (Layer 3)
- **Explanation**: Why pre-launch checklists are insufficient and how production automated judges, member feedback, and sampled traces maintain safety over time.
- **Key claims**:
  - Safety is a continuous evaluation layer that runs the whole time
  - Automated judges must run on live production traffic with multiple dimensions
  - The bottleneck is having enough people to read signals and act on them
- **Examples**:
  - Automated judges checking clinical accuracy, safety, and escalation correctness every few hours
  - Thumbs up/down member feedback on every message
  - 100% sampling on high-stake cases
- **Terminology**:
  - automated judges
  - member feedback
  - sampled traces
  - regression
- **Why it matters**: Proves that monitoring is the first resort for catching new failures and scaling safety with new judges as consumer usage grows.
### The Decisioning Framework (5 Rules for Stakeholder Disagreements)
- **Explanation**: A structured framework for resolving launch disagreements across clinical, legal, compliance, product, and engineering stakeholders.
- **Key claims**:
  - Worst case wins: Severity is set by the worst plausible outcome, not the average
  - Severity does not equal capacity: A bug's severity is determined by harm, not team capacity
  - Asymmetric default: When in doubt, default to the safer mistake
  - Revealed tolerance beats stated tolerance: Align with actual accepted production behavior
  - Humans are the constraint: Always design for the human in the loop
- **Examples**:
  - Comparing safety bugs (always hold and fix) versus polished bugs (ship)
  - Evaluating clinical risk vs velocity risk prior to launch
- **Terminology**:
  - worst case
  - asymmetric default
  - revealed tolerance
  - human in the loop
- **Why it matters**: Resolves organizational deadlock when five different stakeholders see five different risks during product launches.
## Key Points
### Constraint is the Architecture
- **Explanation**: Safety failures stem from architectural design choices made before model deployment, not just model failures.
- **Evidence**: ECRI ranking AI chatbot misuse as the top health tech hazard for 2026.
- **Practical implication**: Architect systems so that PHI is stripped at ingestion and environments are strictly isolated.
### Must-Not-Fail Belongs Above the Prompt
- **Explanation**: Probabilistic models are unreliable for deterministic business logic and critical safety checks.
- **Evidence**: Code layer runs first on every turn; models never get a vote on high-stakes calls.
- **Practical implication**: Implement emergency routing and authentication checks in deterministic code rather than system prompts.
### Safety is Continuous, Not a Gate
- **Explanation**: Pre-launch evaluation checklists are necessary but insufficient for production AI systems.
- **Evidence**: New model versions and prompt changes introduce new failures over time.
- **Practical implication**: Deploy continuous automated judges, live member feedback monitoring, and 100% sampled traces.
### Worst Case Wins in Healthcare Decisions
- **Explanation**: When evaluating bug severity, the worst plausible outcome sets the standard, not the average case.
- **Evidence**: A bug causing serious harm to 0.1% of users is much worse than a minor annoyance to 100%.
- **Practical implication**: Never compromise on safety bugs for velocity; treat fast-follows as committed debt.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### Three-Layer Architecture for Member-Facing Health AI
- **How it works**: Combines policy-enforcing architecture, deterministic code layers for high-stakes logic, and continuous safety evaluation layers in production.
- **Components**:
  - Layer 1: Pipeline sanitization and environment isolation
  - Layer 2: Code layer running above prompts for deterministic safety rules
  - Layer 3: Continuous evaluation layer with automated judges, member feedback, and sampled traces
- **When to use**: When building member-facing healthcare AI or any high-stakes regulated AI application.
### The Five-Rule Decisioning Framework
- **How it works**: A decision-making model to resolve launch blockages when cross-functional stakeholders disagree on risk.
- **Components**:
  - Rule 1: Worst case wins
  - Rule 2: Severity does not equal capacity
  - Rule 3: Asymmetric default (safety first)
  - Rule 4: Revealed tolerance over stated tolerance
  - Rule 5: Humans are the constraint
- **When to use**: When deciding whether to ship, delay, or fix features when clinical, legal, compliance, product, and engineering stakeholders disagree.
## Examples & Case Studies
### A 60-year-old healthy man asked a popular AI assistant how to cut salt and was told to use sodium bromide, leading to hospitalization.
- **Illustrates**: The danger of probabilistic models generating hallucinatory medical advice without deterministic safety boundaries.
- **Lesson**: High-stakes medical guidance cannot be left to probabilistic generation.
### An independent safety test out of Mount Sinai found health AI under-triaged life-threatening emergencies 50% of the time.
- **Illustrates**: Current consumer health AI safety gaps and production baseline risks.
- **Lesson**: Rigorous architectural guardrails and deterministic triage pathways are required.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Sanitize PHI at the pipeline boundary before storage
  - Place deterministic safety rules in code above prompts
  - Evaluate models continuously using live production traffic and automated judges
- **Strategic**:
  - Adopt the worst-case mindset for healthcare AI safety evaluation
  - Align launch decisions with revealed organizational tolerance rather than stated goals
  - Treat fast-follows as committed debt rather than optional backlog items
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - Are our high-stakes safety checks handled in code or left to system prompts?
  - Do we have continuous automated judges evaluating live production traffic?
  - How do we resolve launch disagreements between clinical, legal, and engineering stakeholders?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- 40 million people use frontier models for triaging healthcare issues (statistic)
- ECRI named AI chatbot misuse the number one health technology hazard of 2026 (industry report)
## Notable Quotes
> "So how do you ship AI to someone who has already trusted you with their health?" (at 0:53)
> "A model is not a guardrail. A model with a system prompt is not a guardrail. Code that runs above the model is closer." (at 10:15)
> "Architecture is how. Decisioning is when. Member trust is why." (at 35:02)
## Compressed Summary
- healthcare ai requires strict architectural guardrails and deterministic code layers
- must-not-fail logic like emergency routing must live above prompts in code
- safety is a continuous production evaluation layer using automated judges and member feedback
- the 5-rule decisioning framework resolves stakeholder launch conflicts using worst-case analysis
- **Keywords**: guardrails, healthcare, architecture, safety, decisioning
- **Core insight**: Building trusted healthcare AI requires enforcing non-negotiable safety rules through architecture and deterministic code rather than relying solely on model prompts and probabilistic generation.
